screens.title: Caching Strategies and Eviction Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Caching is one of the most practical levers you have to make systems faster and more resilient. In this chapter we'll build an operational understanding: what caching buys you, the different places you can put a cache in a system, the common read and write strategies, and how eviction and invalidation shape correctness. You'll see concrete examples that show how a cache reduces latency and database load, and we'll step through a Cache-Aside example using Redis with a short time-to-live. As you study, pay attention to trade-offs: a cache can improve performance dramatically, but it adds complexity — you must pick where it lives, how it is populated, and how it is kept fresh. We'll also cover eviction policies like Least Recently Used and Least Frequently Used so you can choose policies that match access patterns. By the end, you'll be able to name the right caching layer, select a read/write strategy, and explain how TTL and explicit invalidation address staleness. Consider: if you add a cache today, what consistency guarantees are you willing to trade for speed?

screens.title: Why Cache? Benefits and trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: At its simplest, caching stores frequently accessed data in a faster temporary location so repeated requests avoid the slower primary store. This yields three practical benefits: lower latency for end users, reduced load on your origin databases, and improved overall throughput under heavy traffic. A concrete example is a social feed: serving cached rendered posts for millions of reads avoids repeated database joins and heavy queries. But caching introduces trade-offs. Cached copies can become stale, so you must decide the acceptable freshness level. Another cost is complexity: instrumenting cache hit rates, handling cache misses gracefully, and designing eviction behavior all take effort. A common misconception is that caches always improve performance — if misconfigured TTLs or no eviction policy lead to stale or bloated caches, they can cause correctness or memory problems. When you choose to cache, measure the delta: compare average response time and origin C P U under load. Finally, always pair caching with observability: track hits, misses, and expired entries so you can tune TTL, eviction policy, and placement. What freshness guarantees does your application require, and how will you measure that they are met?

content.html:
Definition
Caching
Store frequent data in faster storage temporarily so later requests are served without accessing the primary data store.
Benefit: Latency
Cached reads are much faster than repeated database reads.
Benefit: Load reduction
Caches reduce concurrent load on the primary store during spikes.
Cost: Staleness risk
Without eviction, TTL or invalidation, cached data may go out of date.
Concrete Example
Social feed reads
Imagine thousands of users requesting a popular post. Serving the post from cache avoids repeated heavy queries and database CPU, making responses faster and the system more stable under spike. Observe hit vs miss counts to tune TTLs for acceptable freshness.
Misconception
A cache is not a substitute for correct system design. Incorrect invalidation can return stale or incorrect content.
Pro tip
Start with metrics: measure response time and origin load before and after adding a cache to see real impact.
Key Takeaway

Use caching to lower latency and origin load, but design invalidation and eviction intentionally to maintain correctness.

screens.title: Layers of Caching
screens.narratorSegment: Caches exist at multiple layers, and each layer serves different goals. A client-side cache — typically a browser cache — eliminates network calls entirely for static assets and sometimes A P I responses, using HTTP headers like cache-control and ETag. CDNs cache large static and semi-static assets close to users to reduce geographic latency and bandwidth costs. Reverse proxy or load balancer caches sit in front of application servers and can short-circuit repeated requests before application logic executes. Application server caches are in-memory stores local to an instance and offer very fast access at the cost of limited scope. Finally, distributed caches like Redis provide a shared, fast layer accessible by all application instances, solving the consistency problem between replicas. Choosing placement depends on the data's scope and consistency requirements: use client caches and CDNs for static content, application caches for per-instance accelerations, and distributed caches for shared, frequently-read data. A common mistake is using only local caches in a horizontally scaled system, which causes inconsistent behavior across instances. Instead, select a combination: CDN for static assets, distributed cache for shared reads, and instrument each layer to measure hit ratios and freshness.

Client Cache
Browser caching using HTTP headers
Fastest: avoids network calls for repeat visits. Use Cache-Control and ETag for control.
CDN
Edge caching for static and large files
Reduces geographic latency and origin bandwidth. Best for images, videos, and compiled assets.
Reverse Proxy
Nginx or load balancer caching
Short-circuits repeated requests before application logic, saving CPU and latency.
Application Cache
In-memory per instance
Very fast but local — can cause inconsistency across instances if used alone.
Distributed Cache
Shared cache like Redis
Accessible to all instances; essential for horizontal scaling and consistent shared reads.
Why placement matters

Placement determines speed, scope, and how you handle consistency. Match layer to the data's access pattern and freshness needs.

Checklist
  • Is the data global static or per-user?
  • Can stale reads be tolerated?
  • Will you need shared state between instances?

screens.title: Client-Side Cache vs CDN
screens.narratorSegment: Client-side caches and CDNs both reduce latency, but they serve different scopes and operational needs. A browser cache stores resources on the user's device and can completely avoid network requests for repeat visits. This is ideal for static assets and reduces per-user bandwidth, but it depends on correct HTTP caching headers and user behavior. A CDN replicates and caches content at edge locations globally, reducing geographic latency and bandwidth from the origin server. CDNs are better suited to large files or content that must be shared across many users — for example, images, videos, and commonly downloaded assets. A misconception is treating them as interchangeable: browser caching is most effective for returning users and small static files, while a CDN handles global scale and offloads origin bandwidth. Choose both where appropriate — use Cache-Control to let clients cache while also configuring CDN TTLs to control edge freshness. Remember to set explicit invalidation for files that change frequently or use versioned URLs to avoid cache-invalidity problems. Client-Side Cache vs CDN means browser caches optimize per-user repeat access; cdns optimize global delivery and origin bandwidth reduction.. In practical terms, when to rely on browser caching and when to use a cdn edge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Client-Side Cache
Browser caching
Stores assets on the user's device; avoids network calls for repeat visits. Controlled by Cache-Control and ETag headers.
Best for: small static assets and APIs where per-user freshness is acceptable.
Pro tip: version your assets to force updates instead of relying on short TTLs.
CDN
Edge caching
Replicates content across geographic edge nodes to reduce latency and origin bandwidth for many users.
Best for: images, videos, site assets, and any content shared across users.
Misconception: CDNs are not a substitute for versioning; explicit invalidation or versioned URLs are still necessary when updating assets.
Action
Use cache headers for client-side caching and configure CDN TTLs. For frequently changing assets, use versioned URLs to avoid stale caches.

screens.title: Application Server Cache vs Distributed Cache
screens.narratorSegment: Application-level caches are often implemented as in-memory maps inside a server process. They are extremely fast and useful for per-instance speedups — for example, caching computed templates or recently-used configuration. However, when you scale horizontally, local caches create divergence between instances and can lead to inconsistent reads across users. A distributed cache solves that by providing a shared layer that all instances can query. Redis and Memcached are common examples; they run as a separate cluster and allow many app servers to read the same cached entries. The trade-offs are clear: local caches are faster per access but limited by memory and scope, whereas distributed caches add a network round trip but provide consistency and shared state. A misconception is assuming distributed caches always remove inconsistency; they reduce it for reads but you still must design invalidation or write strategies. Instrument hit and miss rates for both caches and prefer distributed caches for session data or shared profiles while using local caches for ephemeral per-instance optimizations. Application Server Cache vs Distributed Cache means local caches give fastest access per instance; distributed caches share state across instances and are essential when horizontal consistency is needed.. In practical terms, local in-memory caches and shared caches like redis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Application Cache
In-memory per instance
Fast but isolated. Use it for computed values and per-instance work where cross-instance consistency is not required.
Use when: speed is critical and data is per-instance or recomputable.
Distributed Cache
Redis or Memcached cluster
Shared between app instances. Adds a network hop but ensures a single coherent cache for reads and shared state.
Use when: sessions, shared profiles, and frequently-read shared objects need fast access across instances.
Example topology
Clients → Load Balancer → App Instances (local cache) → Distributed Cache (Redis) → Database. This lets app instances benefit from local caches while keeping a shared source for cross-instance reads.

screens.title: Caching Strategies Explained
screens.narratorSegment: There are four common caching strategies and each places responsibility differently. Cache-Aside (lazy loading) makes the application the owner: on read it checks the cache, on miss it fetches from the database and populates the cache, and writes go to the database while the application invalidates or updates the cache. Read-Through pushes read responsibility into the cache: the application requests data from the cache and the cache loads from the database on a miss. Write-Through writes synchronously to both cache and database so the cache stays consistent at the cost of slower writes. Write-Back (or write-behind) writes only to the cache and lets the cache asynchronously flush changes to the database, which reduces write latency but risks data loss if the cache fails. A common misconception is assuming write-back always improves performance without downsides; it does reduce write latency but requires strong persistence guarantees or risk of lost writes. Choose Cache-Aside for straightforward control and Read-Through or Write-Through when you want the cache to manage data flow, and use Write-Back only when low write latency is essential and you accept the risk and complexity.

keyIdea.text: Cache-Aside gives application control; Read/Write-Through move responsibility into the cache; Write-Back optimizes write latency at durability risk.

content.html:
Cache-Aside
Application checks cache first; on miss it reads DB and populates cache. Writes go to DB and invalidate cache.
When to use: simple control, explicit invalidation is possible.
Misconception: it doesn't auto-handle cache updates on writes; the app must do it.
Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Back
Read-Through: cache fetches from DB on misses. Write-Through: writes to cache and DB synchronously. Write-Back: write to cache, async flush to DB.
Tradeoffs: Write-Through maintains consistency but raises write latency.
Write-Back: low write latency but risk of data loss if cache fails before persistence.
Decision guide
If you need simple explicit control, pick Cache-Aside. If you want the cache to abstract DB access, consider Read/Write-Through. Use Write-Back only when write latency is critical and you can tolerate complexity.

screens.title: Cache-Aside with Redis — Code Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a Cache-Aside example implemented in Python with Redis. The example simulates a database fetch when the cache misses, prints whether you saw a cache hit or miss, and stores the profile into Redis with a TTL of 60 seconds. Key lines to note: the code tries to get a key from Redis first; if present it decodes JSON and returns the cached object, producing a cache hit. On a miss it calls the simulated fetch function that sleeps to represent database latency, then sets the key using a TTL. This pattern keeps reads fast on subsequent requests and keeps writes anchored in the database. A common misconception is to rely solely on TTLs for correctness; Cached-Aside requires explicit invalidation on writes if you need immediate consistency. In your terminal demo, watch the printed output: the first call should show a cache miss and the simulated DB fetch, the second call a cache hit. If you wait for the TTL to expire, you will observe another miss. This exercise helps you see timing, TTL behavior, and how simple instrumentation reveals hit/miss dynamics.

content.html:
Code Example
Cache-Aside using redis and a simulated DB
import redis
import json
import time

try:
    r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0)
    r.ping()
    print("Connected to Redis successfully!")
except redis.exceptions.ConnectionError as e:
    print(f"Could not connect to Redis: {e}. Please ensure Redis server is running.")
    exit()

def fetch_user_from_database(user_id):
    print(f"  --> Fetching user {user_id} from database...")
    time.sleep(0.5)
    return {"id": user_id, "name": f"User {user_id}", "email": f"user{user_id}@example.com"}

def get_user_profile(user_id):
    cache_key = f"user:{user_id}"
    cached_profile = r.get(cache_key)
    if cached_profile:
        print(f"Cache HIT for {cache_key}")
        return json.loads(cached_profile.decode('utf-8'))
    else:
        print(f"Cache MISS for {cache_key}")
        db_profile = fetch_user_from_database(user_id)
        r.setex(cache_key, 60, json.dumps(db_profile))
        return db_profile

print("--- First call (should be a cache miss) ---")
profile1 = get_user_profile(101)
print(f"Profile: {profile1}")

print("
--- Second call (should be a cache hit) ---")
profile2 = get_user_profile(101)
print(f"Profile: {profile2}")
What to watch
Terminal output shows "Cache MISS" then a DB fetch and later "Cache HIT". Observe timings and TTL behavior by waiting 60 seconds to see expiry.
Misconception
TTL alone is not a substitute for explicit invalidation when writes require immediate consistency.

screens.title: Read-Through vs Write-Through vs Write-Back
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding read and write strategies helps you pick a pattern aligned to your performance and durability needs. Read-Through makes the cache responsible for fetching missing data; it simplifies the application but centralizes logic in the caching layer. Write-Through writes to cache and database synchronously, ensuring the cache is immediately consistent, but every write pays the latency cost of two writes. Write-Back writes only to the cache and flushes to the database asynchronously. This yields low write latency but introduces risk: if the cache fails before persistence, recent writes may be lost. Use Read-Through when you want to hide database reads behind the cache, and Write-Through when you need strong read-after-write consistency. Consider Write-Back only when write latency is a primary constraint and you have durability mechanisms — for example, replication and careful persistence of the cache state. A common misconception is that Write-Back is always better for throughput; it can be faster but increases complexity for correctness and recovery. Always align strategy with the application's tolerance for stale reads and potential data loss. Read-Through vs Write-Through vs Write-Back means pick read/write strategies by balancing simplicity, write latency, and durability requirements.. In practical terms, trade-offs for reads, writes, and durability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Read-Through
Cache fetches from DB on miss. App requests only the cache. Simplifies app logic for reads.
Write-Through
Writes go to cache and DB synchronously. Keeps cache consistent but increases write latency.
Write-Back
Writes are stored in cache and flushed asynchronously to DB. Improves write latency but risks lost writes on failure.
When to use

screens.title: Cache Eviction Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Eviction policies determine which items a cache removes when it reaches capacity. The most common policies are LRU, LFU, FIFO, and Random. LRU — Least Recently Used — evicts items that haven't been accessed for the longest time and works well when recent access predicts future use. LFU — Least Frequently Used — evicts items with the smallest access counts and is useful when a small set of keys are consistently popular over a long period. FIFO evicts the oldest inserted items regardless of access pattern; it's simple but can discard hot items. Random eviction removes arbitrary items and is generally a fallback. Choosing the right policy depends on access characteristics: if your workload has strong temporal locality, LRU is often a good default; if popularity is stable over the long term, LFU may retain the right items. A common mistake is not monitoring the effectiveness of the policy — measure hit rates and simulate growth to ensure your chosen policy matches real access patterns. Also consider combination policies or segmented caches when a single policy doesn't fit the workload.

keyIdea.text: LRU is effective for temporal locality; LFU suits long-term popularity; FIFO is simple but blind to access frequency.

LRU
Evict the least recently used item. Good for temporal locality; keeps recently accessed items longer.
LFU
Evict the least frequently used item. Best when a stable set of keys is popular over time.
FIFO
Evict the oldest inserted item. Simple but may remove hot items unexpectedly.
Random
Evict a random item. Useful as a simple fallback or to avoid pathological structures.
How to choose
Match the policy to access patterns and measure hit rate. When unsure, LRU is a strong default for many web workloads with recency patterns.

screens.title: Cache Invalidation and Staleness
screens.narratorSegment: Cache invalidation is often described as the hardest problem because cached copies can diverge from the source of truth. There are a few common approaches. Time-to-Live (TTL) attaches an expiration to each entry; once expired, the entry is removed or considered stale. TTLs are easy to implement and provide eventual freshness, but choosing the right TTL requires understanding data change frequency. Explicit invalidation is when the application, upon updating the database, also removes or updates the corresponding cache entry. This ensures immediate removal of stale entries but adds work to the write path. Publish/Subscribe involves publishing change events when data updates and having cache services subscribe to those events to invalidate or update entries. This pattern scales to multiple caches and distributed systems but needs reliable event delivery. A typical pitfall is not handling cache misses gracefully: a sudden expiration or manual invalidation can cause many clients to hit the database simultaneously — a cache stampede. Measure and use techniques such as staggered expirations or controlled rebuilds where necessary. Always align invalidation approach with your application's tolerance for stale reads.

When many clients request an expired item simultaneously, the origin can be overwhelmed. Plan for graceful rebuilds and instrument miss bursts.

Pick an invalidation approach consistent with your freshness needs: TTL for eventual, explicit for immediate, pub/sub for distributed systems.

fullNarratorScript:
Caching is one of the most practical levers you have to make systems faster and more resilient. In this chapter we'll build an operational understanding: what caching buys you, the different places you can put a cache in a system, the common read and write strategies, and how eviction and invalidation shape correctness. You'll see concrete examples that show how a cache reduces latency and database load, and we'll step through a Cache-Aside example using Redis with a short time-to-live. As you study, pay attention to trade-offs: a cache can improve performance dramatically, but it adds complexity — you must pick where it lives, how it is populated, and how it is kept fresh. We'll also cover eviction policies like Least Recently Used and Least Frequently Used so you can choose policies that match access patterns. By the end, you'll be able to name the right caching layer, select a read/write strategy, and explain how TTL and explicit invalidation address staleness. Consider: if you add a cache today, what consistency guarantees are you willing to trade for speed?

By the end of this chapter you will explain why caches are used in distributed systems and identify the appropriate layer to place them. You'll also be able to describe the four common caching strategies and evaluate their trade-offs for latency and consistency. Each objective ties to practical decisions: choose a CDN for global static assets, use a distributed cache like Redis for shared session or profile data, or rely on a local application cache for single-instance optimizations. The objectives continue: you will compare eviction policies such as LRU and LFU and select one based on access patterns, and you will reason about cache invalidation using TTLs, explicit invalidation, or publish/subscribe mechanisms. As you practice, measure cache hit rates and simulate expiry scenarios so you can observe cache misses, stampedes, and data staleness. These skills let you protect your database from surges, lower tail latency, and apply a clear consistency posture when fresh data matters.

These additional objectives focus on practical validation and reasoning under failure. You will learn to measure and interpret cache hit rates, understand how TTL affects freshness, and recognize cache stampedes — where many clients request a stale item and overwhelm the origin. We'll also practice explicit invalidation patterns and publish/subscribe invalidation so you can connect cache updates to data changes. Finally, you will know how to simulate expiry and measure the difference in response time between hits and misses. Each of these objectives supports safe deployment: instrument your cache, observe hit ratios, set conservative TTLs when correctness matters, and prefer explicit invalidation for critical writes. As you work through the hands-on exercise, you will see terminal output that highlights cache hit and miss behavior and learn why TTLs are a pragmatic compromise when immediate consistency is not required.

At its simplest, caching stores frequently accessed data in a faster temporary location so repeated requests avoid the slower primary store. This yields three practical benefits: lower latency for end users, reduced load on your origin databases, and improved overall throughput under heavy traffic. A concrete example is a social feed: serving cached rendered posts for millions of reads avoids repeated database joins and heavy queries. But caching introduces trade-offs. Cached copies can become stale, so you must decide the acceptable freshness level. Another cost is complexity: instrumenting cache hit rates, handling cache misses gracefully, and designing eviction behavior all take effort. A common misconception is that caches always improve performance — if misconfigured TTLs or no eviction policy lead to stale or bloated caches, they can cause correctness or memory problems. When you choose to cache, measure the delta: compare average response time and origin C P U under load. Finally, always pair caching with observability: track hits, misses, and expired entries so you can tune TTL, eviction policy, and placement. What freshness guarantees does your application require, and how will you measure that they are met?

Caches exist at multiple layers, and each layer serves different goals. A client-side cache — typically a browser cache — eliminates network calls entirely for static assets and sometimes A P I responses, using HTTP headers like cache-control and ETag. CDNs cache large static and semi-static assets close to users to reduce geographic latency and bandwidth costs. Reverse proxy or load balancer caches sit in front of application servers and can short-circuit repeated requests before application logic executes. Application server caches are in-memory stores local to an instance and offer very fast access at the cost of limited scope. Finally, distributed caches like Redis provide a shared, fast layer accessible by all application instances, solving the consistency problem between replicas. Choosing placement depends on the data's scope and consistency requirements: use client caches and CDNs for static content, application caches for per-instance accelerations, and distributed caches for shared, frequently-read data. A common mistake is using only local caches in a horizontally scaled system, which causes inconsistent behavior across instances. Instead, select a combination: CDN for static assets, distributed cache for shared reads, and instrument each layer to measure hit ratios and freshness.

Client-side caches and CDNs both reduce latency, but they serve different scopes and operational needs. A browser cache stores resources on the user's device and can completely avoid network requests for repeat visits. This is ideal for static assets and reduces per-user bandwidth, but it depends on correct HTTP caching headers and user behavior. A CDN replicates and caches content at edge locations globally, reducing geographic latency and bandwidth from the origin server. CDNs are better suited to large files or content that must be shared across many users — for example, images, videos, and commonly downloaded assets. A misconception is treating them as interchangeable: browser caching is most effective for returning users and small static files, while a CDN handles global scale and offloads origin bandwidth. Choose both where appropriate — use Cache-Control to let clients cache while also configuring CDN TTLs to control edge freshness. Remember to set explicit invalidation for files that change frequently or use versioned URLs to avoid cache-invalidity problems. In practical terms, when to rely on browser caching and when to use a cdn edge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Application-level caches are often implemented as in-memory maps inside a server process. They are extremely fast and useful for per-instance speedups — for example, caching computed templates or recently-used configuration. However, when you scale horizontally, local caches create divergence between instances and can lead to inconsistent reads across users. A distributed cache solves that by providing a shared layer that all instances can query. Redis and Memcached are common examples; they run as a separate cluster and allow many app servers to read the same cached entries. There are four common caching strategies and each places responsibility differently. Cache-Aside (lazy loading) makes the application the owner: on read it checks the cache, on miss it fetches from the database and populates the cache, and writes go to the database while the application invalidates or updates the cache. Read-Through pushes read responsibility into the cache: the application requests data from the cache and the cache loads from the database on a miss. Write-Through writes synchronously to both cache and database so the cache stays consistent at the cost of slower writes. Write-Back (or write-behind) writes only to the cache and lets the cache asynchronously flush changes to the database, which reduces write latency but risks data loss if the cache fails. A common misconception is assuming write-back always improves performance without downsides; it does reduce write latency but requires strong persistence guarantees or risk of lost writes. Choose Cache-Aside for straightforward control and Read-Through or Write-Through when you want the cache to manage data flow, and use Write-Back only when low write latency is essential and you accept the risk and complexity.
